filings.topic: TCP BBR vs CUBIC congestion control
filings.content:
TCP BBR vs CUBIC

CUBIC is loss-based: it grows the congestion window until packets are dropped, then backs off. BBR is model-based: it measures the bottleneck bandwidth and round-trip time, then paces sends to sit at that operating point rather than filling buffers.

How CUBIC works

  • Window growth follows a cubic function of time since the last loss event, so it probes aggressively after a loss and plateaus near the operating point.
  • Its signal for "the path is full" is packet loss, which means it must overfill queues to detect capacity.
  • Consequence: persistent queues in front of the bottleneck — bufferbloat — which raises latency for everyone sharing that link.
  • Loss-based designs also struggle on lossy-but-not-congested paths (wireless errors), where a drop is misread as congestion.

How BBR works

  • Estimates two values: bottleneck bandwidth (BtlBw) and round-trip propagation delay (RTprop).
  • Sends at roughly BtlBw while keeping in-flight data near BtlBw * RTprop (the bandwidth-delay product), so the queue stays small.
  • Periodically probes by slightly increasing or decreasing the send rate to track changes in the path.
  • Because it does not rely on loss as the congestion signal, it tolerates random loss far better and drains standing queues.

Choosing between them

  • BBR tends to keep latency noticeably lower on buffer-bloated or long-fat links, and on paths with random loss.
  • CUBIC can still win on short, high-bandwidth, low-loss paths (e.g. datacenter or LAN transfers), where its loss-based probing is efficient and its buffer-filling behaviour costs little.
  • CUBIC is the Linux default and is friendlier to fair-share expectations; BBR flows can capture more than their share when competing with loss-based flows.

Rule of thumb: loss as a signal (CUBIC) vs. an explicit model of the path (BBR) — the difference is what the sender treats as evidence of congestion.

filings.content:
Direct answer

The CAP theorem says a distributed data store can only guarantee two of three properties — Consistency, Availability, and Partition tolerance — and when a network partition actually occurs it must choose between consistency and availability.

The three properties

  • Consistency (linearizability): every read sees the most recent write or an error; all replicas agree.
  • Availability: every request to a non-failing node gets a response, even if it may be stale.
  • Partition tolerance: the system keeps working despite messages being dropped or delayed between nodes.

Why the choice only bites during a partition

Partitions are unavoidable in real networks, so P is not optional. With no partition, a well-designed system can deliver both C and A. The theorem matters only in the failure window: either refuse some writes/reads to keep replicas in agreement (CP), or keep serving and reconcile the divergence later (AP).

Typical trade-off examples

  • CP: ZooKeeper, etcd, HBase — a minority side loses availability so that committed data stays consistent. Good for locks, leader election, config.
  • AP: Cassandra, DynamoDB-style stores — every node keeps accepting writes; conflicts are resolved with last-writer-wins, vector clocks, or application-level merge. Good for carts, profiles, telemetry.

Common pitfalls

"2-of-3" is a simplification: the real statement is about behaviour during a partition, not a permanent capability cap. PACELC extends it — if partitioned choose A or C, otherwise (else) choose latency or consistency. Also note CAP's consistency is stronger than the C in BASE-style eventual consistency, and network failures are partial, not total, so real systems tune this per operation and per quorum rather than picking one global label.

clawbot.final_text: Created lesson `lesson-6943784810c2` — "LLM Quantization and GGUF Speed" (level working, status open, review 2026-11-19): what quantization is, why fewer bits = less memory traffic/cheaper math, block scale+zero-point representation, GGUF as an mmap-friendly container format, and the quality/speed trade-offs.

filings.content:
Quantization is reducing the numeric precision of a model's weights (and often activations) — e.g. from 16/32-bit floats down to 8, 4, or fewer bits. The model gets smaller and arithmetic gets cheaper, at the cost of a small accuracy drop. GGUF is fast for local inference because it stores those quantized weights in a layout that can be memory-mapped directly, so the file is used almost as-is without a heavy parse/convert step.

Why lower precision makes things faster

  • Less memory traffic. Inference on CPU and consumer GPUs is usually bandwidth-bound: every token requires reading all the weights. Halving the bits per weight roughly halves the bytes that must be moved.
  • Smaller footprint. A 7B model is ~14 GB at FP16 but ~4 GB at 4-bit, so it fits in RAM (or VRAM) that the full-precision model cannot, and more of it stays cached.
  • Cheaper math. Integer dot-products and fused dequantize-multiply kernels beat full FP32 multiply-accumulate per element.
  • Faster load. Fewer bytes to read from disk means quicker startup.

How a quantized weight is represented

w_real  ~=  scale * q + zero_point     # q is a small integer (e.g. 0..15 for 4-bit)

Weights are grouped into blocks, each with its own scale (and sometimes a zero_point). Fine-grained grouping is what keeps the error small despite so few bits. Common schemes you will see as file suffixes: Q4_K_M, Q5_K_M, Q8_0 — higher number = more bits = larger and slower but more accurate; K/Q variants use grouped/quantile tricks, S uses importance-matrix tuning.

Why GGUF specifically

  • Single self-contained file: weights, tokenizer, vocabulary, chat template, and full metadata in key-value pairs.
  • Tensor layout is aligned and mmap-friendly — the OS pages weights in on demand instead of the program copying them into a fresh buffer.
  • Designed for CPU + mixed CPU/GPU inference (llama.cpp lineage), with partial offload of layers to the GPU.
  • It is a container format, not a quantization algorithm — the quantization scheme is chosen when the model is converted.

Trade-offs to remember

  • Aggressive quantization (2–3 bit) degrades reasoning, long-context and multilingual quality more than it degrades simple recall.
  • Speedups are largest when bandwidth-limited (batch size 1, long generations); at large batches compute dominates and the gap narrows.
  • Compare quality at equal model size, not equal bit-width, and always re-test on your own task.

filings.content:
Ada Nest heartbeat escalation mechanism

The Ada Nest heartbeat escalation system prevents unnecessary alerts by implementing a multi-stage failure detection process. Each member node sends regular heartbeat signals to the hub, which monitors their freshness and triggers escalation only after sustained failure.

Heartbeat monitoring stages

  • Normal operation: Member nodes send heartbeats at regular intervals (e.g., every 30 seconds)
  • Stale state: When a member misses N consecutive heartbeats, its state transitions to "stale"
  • Degraded state: After remaining stale for a defined period, the state becomes "degraded"
  • Escalation to page: Only after the degraded window passes without recovery does the system alert you

Purpose of staged escalation

This multi-stage approach filters out transient issues like brief WiFi disconnections, temporary network congestion, or momentary device sleep states. A single missed heartbeat or short connectivity flap won't trigger an alert, preventing notification fatigue while still catching genuine, sustained failures.

Key design principles

  • Resilience to noise: The system tolerates occasional missed beats without false alarms
  • Intentional delay: There's a deliberate waiting period before escalation to allow for self-recovery
  • State persistence: The hub maintains state across restarts to avoid resetting escalation counters
  • Configurable thresholds: N (missed beats) and degraded window durations are tunable parameters

filings.content:
Spaced repetition

Reviewing material at expanding intervals (1d, 3d, 7d, 30d) exploits the spacing effect: each successful recall just before forgetting strengthens retention far more than re-reading. Anki and similar systems schedule the next review from recall quality.
